The government filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) against the Karnataka High Court’s October 12 judgement, which held the enhancement to be constitutionally impermissible. The 32% reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBC) remained unchanged, taking the total to 56%. The legislation was enacted by the former BJP government following recommendations from a commission headed by retired judge HN Nagamohan Das. items.title: The ‘right to nominate’ under DPDP: A statutory right with no statutory procedure
items.summary: As more of a person’s life moves online, a need has emerged to address what happens when an individual dies or is unable to access their digital data due to incapacity. India’s new data protection law attempts to address this through the nomination right but leaves gaps that a data fiduciary must fill to comply with the legislation's objectives. Section 14(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (“ DP Act ”) allows an individual, the data principal, to nominate any other person who may, on the data principal’s death or incapacity, exercise that individual’s statutory rights under the DP Act and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (“ DP Rules ”). The Act grants the nominee broad authority to exercise powers as if stepping into the shoes of the data principal. Does the right to nominate fill the gap it was designed to fill? The gap the provision attempts to fill is genuine, but the machinery to operate it is thin. Further, because the law on whether digital personal data can be considered “property” capable of succession is still undeveloped, it can lead to conflict when an heir stakes a competing claim. items.title: Prompt, proofread, publish: A practitioners' guide to using AI for legal drafting and content
items.summary: After the Pooja Ramesh Singh judgment debacle , the question is no longer whether lawyers should use generative AI. It is how to use it judiciously so every outcome survives a judge, a client and a bar council. This traces back to July 2, 2026, when a Supreme Court bench of Justices PS Narasimha and Alok Aradhe set aside NCLT and NCLAT orders in Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd because they rested on precedents that didn’t even exist in real life. The Court called this out, stating zero tolerance for unverified, hallucinated AI-generated authorities and characterising their citation as misconduct by any advocate. The Court then directed the Bar Council of India to constitute a committee to address the problem. It wasn’t an isolated incident that led the Supreme Court to take a strong stand against AI-generated content. A month earlier, the Supreme Court’s AI committee released the draft Regulations for Use of Artificial Intelligence in Courts, 2026, which require lawyers to disclose AI assistance in pleadings and filings. items.title: Transparency on trial: Mapping courts’ compliance with the RTI Act
items.summary: The effectiveness of the Right to Information (RTI) regime has, in recent years, come under a cloud of uncertainty with commentators pointing at a progressive weakening of RTI mechanisms. Among the concerns are onerous delays in appointments of information commissioners and other officials, rising backlogs and arbitrary rejections of requests by public authorities . The amendment effected to Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act by the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 further exacerbated these concerns as it empowered public authorities to deny information if it qualified as ‘personal information’, without requiring it to be weighed against public interest. While the High Courts and the Supreme Court often find themselves adjudicating upon the failure of government ministries and departments to comply with the RTI Act, the courts themselves are guilty of not adhering to the principles of the Act.
